mantras.anvaya_en: Subject and verb: a speaker label.

comm.t: Medhas speaks for the last time to King Suratha and the merchant Samādhi. The Goddess has given her promises at the end of chapter 12; the seer now draws his teaching to a close, and the frame story begun in chapter 1 is completed.

In the Gita Press pāṭha the chapter is preceded by its own dhyāna: the Goddess shining like the disc of the rising sun, four-armed and three-eyed, holding noose, goad and the gestures of boon and fearlessness (बालार्कमण्डलाभासां … शिवां भजे). The dhyāna and the bīja ॐ that opens this mantra in recitation belong to the pāṭha, not to the Purāṇa.

Past passive participle used as a finite verb (‘has been told’); the agent, ‘by me’, is understood.

mantras.anvaya: भूप, एतत् उत्तमं देवीमाहात्म्यं ते कथितम्। सा देवी एवंप्रभावा, यया इदं जगत् धार्यते।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: a passive statement with a participle (एतत् … कथितम्), and a nominal sentence (सा देवी एवंप्रभावा) with a relative clause (यया … धार्यते).
mantras.lit: This supreme greatness of the Goddess has been told to you, O king. Of such power is that Goddess by whom this world is upheld.
mantras.tr: I have told you, O king, this supreme account of the Goddess’s greatness. Such is the power of the Goddess by whom this world is sustained.
mantras.tr_note: The passive कथितम् (‘has been told’) is rendered actively, ‘I have told’, with the understood agent supplied.

comm.t: Medhas closes his narrative. The compound देवीमाहात्म्यम् here names what he has told — the greatness of the Goddess — and it is the name the whole text bears in its colophons (देवीमाहात्म्ये).

The verse joins two of her works: she has shown her power in the three stories, and she sustains (धार्यते) the world. Medhas had said the same in 12.36: she, though eternal, comes forth again and again to protect the world.

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (its first member भगवद्विष्णु is a karmadhāraya: भगवान् चासौ विष्णुः च)
samasa.literal: by the māyā of the blessed Viṣṇu
samasa.sense: by the Goddess as Viṣṇu’s Māyā — Medhas’s first name for her (1.54–55: योगनिद्रा जगत्पतेः, महामाया हरेः)
samasa.alt: Also a karmadhāraya, भगवती चासौ विष्णुमाया च, with भगवती shortened to भगवत् as first member (masculine form of the stem in a karmadhāraya): ‘by the blessed Viṣṇumāyā’ (cf. 5.14, विष्णुमायेति शब्दिता). Either way the agent is the Goddess; the first follows Medhas’s own wording in chapter 1.

morph.note: Passive present of √कृ: the root becomes क्रि- before the passive -य- (क्रियते, ‘is made’).
विवेकिन्, an -in possessive (‘having discrimination’); nom. pl. विवेकिनः, like ज्ञानिनः in 1.49–50.

mantras.anvaya: भगवद्विष्णुमायया तथा एव विद्या क्रियते। तया त्वम्, एषः वैश्यः च, तथा एव अन्ये विवेकिनः (13.4: मोह्यन्ते …)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is a complete passive sentence. The second line names the subjects of the verbs in 13.4 (तया … मोह्यन्ते): the sentence runs on.
mantras.lit: Knowledge, likewise, is brought about by the Māyā of the blessed Viṣṇu. By her you, this merchant, and likewise other men of discernment —
mantras.tr: And knowledge, too, is wrought by the same Māyā of the Lord Viṣṇu. By her you and this merchant, and other discerning men as well,
mantras.tr_note: The sentence of the second line is completed in 13.4.

comm.t: Medhas returns to the question with which the king began (1.40–45): why do men who know better remain bound? The answer is the one given in chapter 1: Viṣṇu’s Māyā. Here he adds the other side — knowledge too (विद्या) is her work.

The verse restates 1.57–58: she is the supreme knowledge (विद्या परमा), the cause of release, and also the cause of the bondage of saṃsāra. Delusion and knowledge come from one power; that is why the remedy proposed in 13.4 is to take refuge in her.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also calls her Viṣṇumāyā (name 339, विष्णुमाया) and Vidyā (name 549, विद्या). The shared names reflect a common Śākta idea; the texts are separate.

flags.uncertain: विद्या तथैव क्रियते is the Gita Press reading; its sense (‘knowledge too is made by her’) is taken from the parallel in 1.57–58. Some printed texts are reported to read तयैव (‘by her alone’); this was not checked against a witness here.

mantras.anvaya: (तया त्वम् एषः वैश्यः च अन्ये विवेकिनः) मोह्यन्ते, मोहिताः च एव, अपरे च मोहम् एष्यन्ति। महाराज, तां परमेश्वरीं शरणम् उपैहि।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes 13.3: three verbs in three tenses (मोह्यन्ते, मोहिताः, एष्यन्ति). The plural verb includes त्वम् among third-person subjects, a loose agreement common in Purāṇic verse. The second line is an imperative with a predicative accusative (शरणम्).
mantras.lit: — are deluded, and have been deluded, and others will go into delusion. Go, O great king, to her, the supreme Sovereign, as refuge.
mantras.tr: are deluded now; others have been deluded, and others yet will fall into delusion. Take refuge, great king, in her, the supreme Sovereign.
mantras.tr_note: The three tenses are distributed over different people for clarity; the Sanskrit lists the verbs without naming separate subjects for the first two.

comm.t: The teaching ends in counsel. Delusion is universal — present, past and future — and even the discerning are not exempt. The remedy is not argument but refuge: ‘go to her’.

Taking refuge (शरणागति) is the step that leads to the austerities of 13.8–12. The king had asked who Mahāmāyā is (1.60); the answer has filled twelve chapters, and its practical conclusion is this imperative.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has परमेश्वरी as name 396. The title is common to Śākta hymns; nothing more specific is implied.

mantras.anvaya_en: A nominal sentence: subject सा, predicate भोगस्वर्गापवर्गदा; the participle आराधिता gives the condition.
mantras.lit: She alone, propitiated, is the giver to men of enjoyment, heaven and release.
mantras.tr: Worshipped, she alone grants to men enjoyment, heaven and final liberation.

comm.t: Medhas’s last words. The worship he recommends is not for one goal only: the same Goddess gives worldly enjoyment, heaven and release. The rest of the chapter shows two of these at once — a kingdom for Suratha, knowledge for the merchant.
अपवर्ग is final liberation (mokṣa). The tradition reads the pair of seekers through this verse: one asks for bhoga, the other for apavarga, and both are granted (13.17–25).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the closely parallel name स्वर्गापवर्गदा (name 764), ‘giver of heaven and release’. The phrase is shared Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.
